entry.content:
Happy AI Agenda Live day! For those joining us today at SFMOMA, I’m so excited to meet you all and talk about this exciting, if slightly contentious, moment in the AI industry.

Our staff and attendees will ask top researchers, founders and executives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Nvidia some burning questions. Here are three at the top of my mind.

entry.title: Founders Fund, Khosla Ventures Visit China as Country’s AI Prowess Rises
entry.content:
U.S. venture capitalists have slashed investments in Chinese startups in recent years as relations between the two superpowers have soured. But behind the scenes, plenty are taking weekslong trips to meet with the country’s tech founders—a sign of the influence Chinese startups like DeepSeek wield in the hottest parts of tech.

Last month, three partners at Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund—Sean Liu, John Luttig and Joey Krug—visited tech companies in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. It was the second trip to China Liu had made in the past year and Luttig’s first visit to the country, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter. The idea was not to make investments but to learn about China’s thriving tech sector.

entry.title: Anthropic in Talks to Cement Control Over More Data Centers
entry.content:
Anthropic is in early talks to lease up to 1 gigawatt in compute capacity from a data center developer majority-owned by Apollo Global Management, part of a major effort by the AI company to reduce its reliance on cloud providers.

The maker of Claude has discussed signing on as a direct tenant of sites developed by Stream Data Centers, a 27-year-old company with facilities across the U.S., and filling them with tensor processing units designed by Broadcom and Google, according to people with knowledge of the discussions.

entry.title: AI, the UN, Xi and Trump
entry.content:
It’s a big week for global leaders talking about AI. We’ve got a bunch of presidents and prime ministers at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York—motorcades are creating chaos in Midtown Manhattan right now—and Chinese president Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington tomorrow. The top executives from most big tech firms will be at a state dinner on Thursday night with Xi, while some will also be at the U.N. earlier in the week.

You can bet AI will dominate much of the discussion both at the U.N. and in Washington. It’s unlikely anything of substance will emerge, although there’ll be plenty of breathless headlines. On Tuesday morning, for instance, President Donald Trump made news by pronouncing that artificial intelligence would henceforth be known as super intelligence in U.S. government paperwork, because the word “artificial” makes AI sound “fake.” (See below for more on this.) Glad to see the leader of the free world is staying on top of the most important issues!

entry.title: Barrick Gold Inks Five-Year AI Deal Before IPO
entry.content:
AI is top of mind for stock investors these days. That means even companies outside tech are beefing up their AI credentials ahead of new listings. 

In one such example, Barrick Gold’s North American unit has agreed to a five-year partnership with Avathon, a startup that develops AI-powered software to help industrial companies predict when expensive equipment will fail and monitors mine and factories sites for safety risks, Avathon CEO Pervinder Johar told me. 

Barrick is planning to float a minority stake in its North American unit, which produces the majority of its gold. The company has targeted year-end for the listing.

entry.title: Wall Street’s GPU Futures Push Stalls at the CFTC
entry.content:
The launch of futures for rental prices on Nvidia GPUs, which are seen as important to make AI compute an investable asset class, is hitting a snag.

CME Group had hoped to launch contracts as soon as early October, but it won’t have regulatory approval by then. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates the futures market, is extending its review as it digs into how such contracts work and seeks comments from the broader industry, according to a letter to the exchange seen by The Information.

entry.title: New Data Show Anthropic, OpenAI and Other Upstarts Are Eating into Software Budgets
entry.content:
We’ve been reporting for months about how companies are shifting some traditional software spending to Anthropic and OpenAI. New data from procurement software firm Zip provides further evidence.

AI providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, and Sierra accounted for 8% of spending by Zip customers in the 12 months that ended in August, up from 1.4% during the previous 12 months. Overall, their software budgets rose by a median of 13% during that period. 

The dozens of customers included in the study had an average of 2,400 employees and spent $18 billion for software, including AI, over the past four years. Zip’s customers include Snowflake, OpenAI, Datadog, Cloudflare and AMD.

entry.title: Why America’s AI Dream Is Failing to Launch
entry.content:
In 2022, American dominance in AI looked almost unassailable. The U.S. led in advanced models, semiconductors, capital and talent. Its closest competitor, China, appeared to be reeling from export controls that cut it off from the world’s most advanced process nodes, chips and memory technologies.

Four years later, the tide seems to be turning. Chinese models have gained major global token share; American technology giants are eyeing Chinese logic and memory chips; and America’s grand AI ambitions face growing public backlash.

During the first three months of 2026, local opposition blocked or delayed roughly $130 billion in data center projects. This spring, 71% of Americans surveyed opposed the construction of a data center near where they live. Texas, the fastest-growing state in data center construction, has frozen new grid-connected projects until further impact studies are completed. Data centers have become a bipartisan sleeper issue for the election cycle.

entry.title: Luckey’s Erebor Bank Plots Syria Expansion
entry.content:
Erebor Bank, fresh from becoming a vital new financial bridge between the U.S. and Venezuela, is eyeing a new foreign foray: expanding into Syria.

The bank, founded by Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, has told staff and some investors it could help the war-torn Middle Eastern country reconnect to the global financial system, potentially attracting billions in deposits from businesses and consumers, according to people familiar with the strategy. Doing so would make Erebor a remarkably early mover in Syria, given that Washington only recently reopened the country to U.S. firms and investment.

entry.title: Entertainment-Booking Startup Ande Raises $52 Million From Lightspeed, Redpoint
entry.content:
Personal AI agents like Instinct and Muse have promised to take away the hassle of booking hard-to-get restaurant reservations, Broadway tickets and sporting events. Now, a startup is coming out of stealth to do the same for corporate entertainment—events, group dining, catering, sporting events and more. 

Ande, founded nearly three years ago, says its AI agents help businesses arrange events for employees or customers, handling everything from booking a venue to processing expenses, CEO Lohit Sarma said. The firm’s customers include Cloudflare, Salesforce and McGraw Hill.

The New York-based startup has raised more than $52 million in funding across seed and Series A rounds from Lightspeed Venture Partners, Redpoint Ventures, Duration Ventures, Sierra Ventures and Bain Capital Ventures, Sarma told The Information exclusively. He declined to disclose the valuation.
